transitionIn.text: About 1150 BC. Egypt's empire is gone from Canaan. Philistine cities lie on the coast, Israelite villages in the hills, and Jewish tradition remembers this as the age of the Judges.
transitionIn.title: c. 1150 BC: villages, judges and the first kings

steps.text: The Long Map. The Story of the Jews. Villages, judges, and the first kings.
It is about eleven hundred and fifty BC. Egypt's rule in Canaan is ending, and no great power holds the land.
claims: It is about eleven hundred and fifty BC. Egypt's rule in Canaan is ending, and no great power holds the land.
steps.display: It is about 1150 BC. Egypt's rule in Canaan is ending, and no great power holds the land.

vignette.alt: An empty mud-brick fort with round towers and an open gate
vignette.caption: An empty Egyptian fort (impression)

steps.text: On the southern coast, the Philistines are building up their cities.
claims: On the southern coast, the Philistines are building up their cities.

vignette.alt: Workers laying stone foundations and moulding bricks near the sea
vignette.caption: Building on the coast (impression)

steps.text: In the hill country, small farming villages keep spreading. Most scholars see in them the beginnings of Israel.
claims: In the hill country, small farming villages keep spreading.
Most scholars see in them the beginnings of Israel.

vignette.alt: Wooded hills with thin columns of smoke rising from scattered villages
vignette.caption: Villages spread (impression)

steps.text: Jewish tradition calls this the age of the Judges. In those days there was no king in Israel.
claims: Jewish tradition calls this the age of the Judges. In those days there was no king in Israel.

steps.text: By about one thousand BC, the Bible tells of kings. First Saul, then David. How much of that story is history is one of the great debates in archaeology.
claims: By about one thousand BC, the Bible tells of kings. First Saul, then David.
How much of that story is history is one of the great debates in archaeology.
steps.display: By about 1000 BC, the Bible tells of kings. First Saul, then David. How much of that story is history is one of the great debates in archaeology.

steps.text: That is the world of this year. You can stay with the story, or explore the map on your own.

transitionOut.text: Next: the Philistine cities, Shiloh and the Judges, Saul and David. Tradition and archaeology are told side by side, and where scholars disagree, each view is given.

explore.text: Open each key place or people on the map to read its fact box. Unexplored ones glow; explored ones get a check. Your progress is saved on this device. When you are ready, press Play to move on to c. 1000 BC.

play.title: From c. 1150 BC to c. 1000 BC
play.intro: Plays full screen like a short narrated film, with subtitles (CC). Pause, step back or forward, or change speed at any time. Stop whenever you like: it remembers your chapter.

steps.text: The Bible speaks of five Philistine lords, ruling five cities. Gaza, Ashkelon and Ashdod near the sea. Ekron and Gath further inland.
claims: The Bible speaks of five Philistine lords, ruling five cities. Gaza, Ashkelon and Ashdod near the sea. Ekron and Gath further inland.

vignette.alt: A walled town on a coastal hill above palms and the sea
vignette.caption: Gaza (impression)

steps.text: Excavations at Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath show the newcomers' culture clearly. Ekron, at Tel Miqne, grew into a large planned city.
claims: Excavations at Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath show the newcomers' culture clearly. Ekron, at Tel Miqne, grew into a large planned city.

vignette.alt: Bird's-eye view of a walled city laid out in regular blocks
vignette.caption: A planned Philistine city (idealised impression)

steps.text: Over time their pottery changed. Painted in red and black, it mixed Aegean, Canaanite and Egyptian styles. Archaeologists call it Bichrome ware.
claims: Over time their pottery changed. Painted in red and black, it mixed Aegean, Canaanite and Egyptian styles. Archaeologists call it Bichrome ware.

vignette.alt: Pottery painted in red and black bands, spirals and birds
vignette.caption: Bichrome ware

steps.text: Further north, at Tell Qasile, in today's Tel Aviv, the Philistines built a temple, and rebuilt it larger more than once.
claims: Further north, at Tell Qasile, in today's Tel Aviv, the Philistines built a temple, and rebuilt it larger more than once.

vignette.alt: Inside a small temple: two wooden pillars, benches along the walls and a raised platform
vignette.caption: The temple at Tell Qasile (artist's impression)

steps.text: Imagine the harbour towns in those years. Potters at their wheels, fishing boats pulled up on the sand, and many languages in the market.

vignette.alt: A harbour town: a potter at the wheel, fishing boats on the sand and a busy market
vignette.caption: A harbour town (artist's impression)

steps.text: Egypt's own strength kept fading. By about ten seventy BC, the line of the Ramesside kings had ended, and Egypt was split between rulers in the north and the priests of Amun at Thebes.
claims: Egypt's own strength kept fading. By about ten seventy BC, the line of the Ramesside kings had ended, and Egypt was split between rulers in the north and the priests of Amun at Thebes.
steps.display: Egypt's own strength kept fading. By about 1070 BC, the line of the Ramesside kings had ended, and Egypt was split between rulers in the north and the priests of Amun at Thebes.

vignette.alt: Priests in white carrying a sacred boat shrine between temple columns, incense smoke
vignette.caption: Priests at Thebes (impression)

steps.text: An Egyptian tale shows how far its fame had fallen. A temple official, Wenamun, sails to Byblos to buy cedar. At Dor, a harbour of a people called the Tjeker, he is robbed. In Byblos, the prince makes him wait for weeks.
claims: An Egyptian tale shows how far its fame had fallen. A temple official, Wenamun, sails to Byblos to buy cedar. At Dor, a harbour of a people called the Tjeker, he is robbed. In Byblos, the prince makes him wait for weeks.

vignette.alt: Cedar logs stacked on the shore of a harbour, a ship waiting offshore
vignette.caption: Cedar at Byblos (artist's impression)

steps.text: Whether Wenamun's story is a real report or a literary tale is debated. Either way, it pictures an Egypt that no longer commands its neighbours.
claims: Whether Wenamun's story is a real report or a literary tale is debated. Either way, it pictures an Egypt that no longer commands its neighbours.

steps.text: Far to the east, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser the First fought the Arameans again and again, and marched to the Mediterranean.
claims: Far to the east, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser the First fought the Arameans again and again, and marched to the Mediterranean.
steps.display: Far to the east, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser I fought the Arameans again and again, and marched to the Mediterranean.

vignette.alt: An army with chariots marching past a burning town by a river
vignette.caption: An Assyrian army (impression)

steps.text: In this world without an empire, small peoples had room to grow. On the coast, the Philistines. Inland, the Arameans. And in the hills, Israel.
claims: In this world without an empire, small peoples had room to grow. On the coast, the Philistines. Inland, the Arameans. And in the hills, Israel.

steps.text: The Book of Judges tells of leaders who rose in times of danger. Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Each saves one tribe or a few. Then the people forget, and trouble returns.
claims: The Book of Judges tells of leaders who rose in times of danger. Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Each saves one tribe or a few. Then the people forget, and trouble returns.

vignette.alt: At night, men on a hill blow ram's horns and hold up torches above a camp
vignette.caption: Gideon's torches (impression)

steps.text: Most scholars think the book was edited centuries later, as part of a longer history that runs from Deuteronomy to Kings.
claims: Most scholars think the book was edited centuries later, as part of a longer history that runs from Deuteronomy to Kings.

steps.text: Some of its stories may keep old memories of tribes and local heroes. How much, no one can say for sure.
claims: Some of its stories may keep old memories of tribes and local heroes. How much, no one can say for sure.

steps.text: What archaeology shows fits a land of villages. No palaces, few town walls, and no sign of a central government in the hills.
claims: What archaeology shows fits a land of villages. No palaces, few town walls, and no sign of a central government in the hills.

steps.text: One place stands out in the tradition. Shiloh, in the hills north of Jerusalem. Here, the Bible says, the Ark of the Covenant was kept, in a sanctuary served by the priest Eli.
claims: One place stands out in the tradition. Shiloh, in the hills north of Jerusalem. Here, the Bible says, the Ark of the Covenant was kept, in a sanctuary served by the priest Eli.

vignette.alt: A tent sanctuary inside a fenced court on a hill, smoke rising from an altar
vignette.caption: Shiloh (impression)

steps.text: Here a woman named Hannah prayed for a child, so quietly that only her lips moved. Her son Samuel grew up at the sanctuary, and became a prophet.
claims: Here a woman named Hannah prayed for a child, so quietly that only her lips moved. Her son Samuel grew up at the sanctuary, and became a prophet.

vignette.alt: A woman in a head-cloth praying silently beside a tent curtain
vignette.caption: Hannah prays (impression)

steps.text: The rabbis of the Talmud took Hannah's silent prayer as a model for how to pray. Her story is read in synagogues on the Jewish New Year.
claims: The rabbis of the Talmud took Hannah's silent prayer as a model for how to pray. Her story is read in synagogues on the Jewish New Year.

steps.text: Excavations at Shiloh found a settlement of this time, with pillared buildings and storerooms full of large jars. Then it burned.
claims: Excavations at Shiloh found a settlement of this time, with pillared buildings and storerooms full of large jars. Then it burned.

vignette.alt: A storeroom with stone pillars and rows of large jars
vignette.caption: A storeroom full of jars (artist's impression)

steps.text: Radiocarbon dates from charred grain in the burned rooms point to the second half of the eleventh century BC.
claims: Radiocarbon dates from charred grain in the burned rooms point to the second half of the eleventh century BC.
steps.display: Radiocarbon dates from charred grain in the burned rooms point to the second half of the 11th century BC.

vignette.alt: Burnt grain spilled from broken jars below a scorched stone wall
vignette.caption: Charred grain (impression)

steps.text: The Bible tells how Israel lost a battle to the Philistines near Aphek, and how the Ark was captured. It was carried to Ashdod, then Gath, then Ekron, and in the end sent back.
claims: The Bible tells how Israel lost a battle to the Philistines near Aphek, and how the Ark was captured. It was carried to Ashdod, then Gath, then Ekron, and in the end sent back.

vignette.alt: Warriors carrying off a chest on poles across a battlefield
vignette.caption: The Ark is taken (impression)

steps.text: The Bible never describes Shiloh's fall. But centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah warned: go to Shiloh, and see what I did to it.
claims: The Bible never describes Shiloh's fall. But centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah warned: go to Shiloh, and see what I did to it.

vignette.alt: Tumbled stone walls overgrown on a hill, a lone olive tree
vignette.caption: Shiloh in ruins (impression)

steps.text: Many scholars link the burnt settlement to these wars with the Philistines. Who set the fire, we do not know.
claims: Many scholars link the burnt settlement to these wars with the Philistines. Who set the fire, we do not know.

steps.text: Imagine the news reaching a hill village. A runner on the path, and people gathering to hear.

vignette.alt: A small figure running along a hill path towards a village where people gather
vignette.caption: News reaches a village (artist's impression)

steps.text: In the story, Samuel now leads the people. But they ask him for something new. Give us a king, to judge us, like all the nations.
claims: In the story, Samuel now leads the people. But they ask him for something new. Give us a king, to judge us, like all the nations.

vignette.alt: Bearded elders in robes speaking to an old man on a village path
vignette.caption: The elders ask (impression)

steps.text: Samuel warns them. A king will take your sons for his chariots, and the best of your fields for his servants. But the people insist.
claims: Samuel warns them. A king will take your sons for his chariots, and the best of your fields for his servants. But the people insist.

vignette.alt: A chariot with officers, men hauling loads, people working the fields
vignette.caption: The way of a king (impression)

steps.text: So Samuel anoints Saul, a tall young man of the tribe of Benjamin, from Gibeah. His first victory, the story says, is to rescue the town of Jabesh-Gilead.
claims: So Samuel anoints Saul, a tall young man of the tribe of Benjamin, from Gibeah. His first victory, the story says, is to rescue the town of Jabesh-Gilead.

vignette.alt: An old man pouring oil from a horn over a young man's head at sunset
vignette.caption: Saul is anointed (impression)

steps.text: Where Gibeah lay is debated. It has long been placed at Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem, but some scholars now look elsewhere.
claims: Where Gibeah lay is debated. It has long been placed at Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem, but some scholars now look elsewhere.

vignette.alt: A hill with a small stone tower above terraced slopes
vignette.caption: Gibeah (impression)

steps.text: No inscription from the time names Saul. Still, many historians think a real highland ruler stands behind the story.
claims: No inscription from the time names Saul.
Still, many historians think a real highland ruler stands behind the story.

steps.text: Israel Finkelstein, for one, argues that Saul led an early territorial kingdom, centred in the hills north of Jerusalem.
claims: Israel Finkelstein, for one, argues that Saul led an early territorial kingdom, centred in the hills north of Jerusalem.

steps.text: The Bible describes a troubled reign. War with the Philistines, quarrels with Samuel, and a dark mood that only music could calm.
claims: The Bible describes a troubled reign. War with the Philistines, quarrels with Samuel, and a dark mood that only music could calm.

vignette.alt: A brooding man seated by a hearth while a young man plays a lyre
vignette.caption: David plays for Saul (impression)

steps.text: The music came from a young shepherd from Bethlehem. His name was David.
claims: The music came from a young shepherd from Bethlehem. His name was David.

vignette.alt: A young shepherd with a staff sitting above grazing sheep, birds overhead
vignette.caption: A shepherd boy (impression)

steps.text: David's own family story crosses borders. The Book of Ruth says his great-grandmother was Ruth, a woman from Moab, who chose to join Israel. Your people shall be my people.
claims: David's own family story crosses borders. The Book of Ruth says his great-grandmother was Ruth, a woman from Moab, who chose to join Israel. Your people shall be my people.

vignette.alt: Women gathering sheaves of barley in a harvest field
vignette.caption: Ruth gleans (impression)

steps.text: Saul's end came in battle on Mount Gilboa, against the Philistines. Saul and his son Jonathan fell, and their bodies were hung on the wall of Beth-Shean.
claims: Saul's end came in battle on Mount Gilboa, against the Philistines. Saul and his son Jonathan fell, and their bodies were hung on the wall of Beth-Shean.

vignette.alt: A dusty battle on a mountain slope, a fallen shield, vultures circling
vignette.caption: Mount Gilboa (impression)

steps.text: David's lament for them is one of the Bible's great poems. Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely, in life and in death they were not divided. How the mighty have fallen.
claims: David's lament for them is one of the Bible's great poems. Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely, in life and in death they were not divided. How the mighty have fallen.

steps.text: The Bible's David is a hero with flaws. He fells the Philistine giant Goliath in the Valley of Elah, flees from Saul, and for a time even serves Achish, king of Gath.
claims: The Bible's David is a hero with flaws. He fells the Philistine giant Goliath in the Valley of Elah, flees from Saul, and for a time even serves Achish, king of Gath.

vignette.alt: A broad valley between low hills, with a dry streambed and scattered trees
vignette.caption: The Valley of Elah (landscape impression)

steps.text: After Saul's death, he is made king at Hebron. Later he takes Jerusalem, and makes it his capital.
claims: After Saul's death, he is made king at Hebron. Later he takes Jerusalem, and makes it his capital.

vignette.alt: A crowd gathering below a hill town among vineyards
vignette.caption: Hebron (impression)

steps.text: Counting back from later kings, the usual reckoning places David around one thousand BC. The exact years are uncertain.
claims: Counting back from later kings, the usual reckoning places David around one thousand BC. The exact years are uncertain.
steps.display: Counting back from later kings, the usual reckoning places David around 1000 BC. The exact years are uncertain.

steps.text: Archaeology has added new evidence. Above the Valley of Elah stands Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town of about two point three hectares, with a double wall and two gates.
claims: Archaeology has added new evidence. Above the Valley of Elah stands Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town of about two point three hectares, with a double wall and two gates.
steps.display: Archaeology has added new evidence. Above the Valley of Elah stands Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town of about 2.3 hectares, with a double wall and two gates.

vignette.alt: A hilltop town ringed by a double stone wall with gates, above a valley
vignette.caption: Khirbet Qeiyafa (stylised impression)

steps.text: It was short-lived. Radiocarbon dates place its destruction around one thousand BC, give or take a few decades.
claims: It was short-lived. Radiocarbon dates place its destruction around one thousand BC, give or take a few decades.
steps.display: It was short-lived. Radiocarbon dates place its destruction around 1000 BC, give or take a few decades.

steps.text: Among its finds were a pottery sherd with five lines of ink writing, and no pig bones.
claims: Among its finds were a pottery sherd with five lines of ink writing, and no pig bones.
steps.display: Among its finds were a pottery sherd with 5 lines of ink writing, and no pig bones.

vignette.alt: A broken pottery sherd with faint lines of ink writing
vignette.caption: An inscribed sherd (impression, not the real text)

steps.text: The writing is hard to read. Some read it as early Hebrew. Others say neither the script nor the language can be pinned down.
claims: The writing is hard to read. Some read it as early Hebrew. Others say neither the script nor the language can be pinned down.

steps.text: Who built the town is debated too. Its excavator, Yosef Garfinkel, sees a stronghold of Judah in David's time. Israel Finkelstein and Alexander Fantalkin link it instead to an early kingdom in the north, perhaps Saul's.
claims: Who built the town is debated too. Its excavator, Yosef Garfinkel, sees a stronghold of Judah in David's time. Israel Finkelstein and Alexander Fantalkin link it instead to an early kingdom in the north, perhaps Saul's.

steps.text: At Gath, a sherd from about this time, or a little later, carries two names that were probably not Semitic. Its excavators note that they recall the name Goliath, but warn that this is not evidence for Goliath himself.
claims: At Gath, a sherd from about this time, or a little later, carries two names that were probably not Semitic. Its excavators note that they recall the name Goliath, but warn that this is not evidence for Goliath himself.

vignette.alt: A broken sherd with two scratched words lying in the dirt
vignette.caption: Gath sherd (not the real text)

steps.text: The first mention of David outside the Bible comes more than a century later. In the ninth century BC, an Aramaean king set up a victory stone at Dan, in the far north.
claims: The first mention of David outside the Bible comes more than a century later. In the ninth century BC, an Aramaean king set up a victory stone at Dan, in the far north.
steps.display: The first mention of David outside the Bible comes more than a century later. In the 9th century BC, an Aramaean king set up a victory stone at Dan, in the far north.

images.alt: A basalt victory stone with carved lines standing at a city gate
images.caption: A victory stone at Dan (impression; it was found broken)

images.alt: Sepia photograph of the real Tel Dan Stele: broken basalt fragments with Aramaic letters, in a museum
images.caption: Real fragments · photo Gary Todd, CC0

steps.text: He boasts of killing a king of Israel, and a king of the House of David. Most scholars read House of David as the name of Judah's royal line, called after its founder.
claims: He boasts of killing a king of Israel, and a king of the House of David.
Most scholars read House of David as the name of Judah's royal line, called after its founder.

steps.text: So how great was David's kingdom? Here scholars divide. Philip Davies and Thomas Thompson argued that the biblical David is mostly the creation of much later writers.
claims: So how great was David's kingdom? Here scholars divide. Philip Davies and Thomas Thompson argued that the biblical David is mostly the creation of much later writers.

steps.text: At the other end, Kenneth Kitchen held that the biblical account is broadly reliable.
claims: At the other end, Kenneth Kitchen held that the biblical account is broadly reliable.

steps.text: Many stand in between. William Dever and Amihai Mazar see a real David, ruling a modest early state. Israel Finkelstein sees a highland chief, ruling from a small Jerusalem.
claims: Many stand in between. William Dever and Amihai Mazar see a real David, ruling a modest early state. Israel Finkelstein sees a highland chief, ruling from a small Jerusalem.

steps.text: Part of the argument is about dates. A shift of a few decades in dating pottery decides whether some large buildings belong to David's time, or to kings a century later.
claims: Part of the argument is about dates. A shift of a few decades in dating pottery decides whether some large buildings belong to David's time, or to kings a century later.

steps.text: In Jerusalem, Eilat Mazar believed she had found David's palace. Other archaeologists dispute her dating of the walls.
claims: In Jerusalem, Eilat Mazar believed she had found David's palace. Other archaeologists dispute her dating of the walls.

steps.text: Imagine the gate at Qeiyafa at dawn. Sentries looking down into the valley, and the smell of bread from the houses.

vignette.alt: A stone town gate at dawn, sentries on the wall looking over the valley, smoke from houses
vignette.caption: The gate at dawn (artist's impression)

steps.text: Large or small, in the Bible the House of David rules Jerusalem for about four hundred years. And in Jewish tradition, David's name became a lasting hope, of a future king who brings peace.
claims: Large or small, in the Bible the House of David rules Jerusalem for about four hundred years. And in Jewish tradition, David's name became a lasting hope, of a future king who brings peace.
steps.display: Large or small, in the Bible the House of David rules Jerusalem for about 400 years. And in Jewish tradition, David's name became a lasting hope, of a future king who brings peace.

steps.text: But the story goes on. In the Bible, David's son Solomon builds a temple in Jerusalem, and after him the kingdom splits in two. That is our next chapter.
claims: In the Bible, David's son Solomon builds a temple in Jerusalem, and after him the kingdom splits in two.
